analysis.one_liner: Hands fracking regulation entirely to the states, blocking federal rules even on federal land.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its Senate committee referral, ending the Congress with 9 Republican cosponsors and no vote of any kind.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have given states the only authority to regulate hydraulic fracturing ("fracking"), including wells drilled on federal land inside a state's borders. That would have stripped the Interior Department and the EPA of any role in writing or enforcing fracking rules, including the first federal fracking rules for public lands that Interior had announced it was preparing in 2011. The bill was referred to the Senate Energy Committee the day it was introduced and never received a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas drillers, and to a lesser extent geothermal producers, would gain by following a single set of state rules instead of facing a second, federal set of standards for fracking — including on federal land, where the Interior Department was preparing the first uniform federal rules. State oil and gas regulators would gain sole permitting authority.

how_it_helps.text: Would have made state rules the only rules that apply to fracking, so drillers would avoid complying with both state and federal standards, including on federal land.
Would have preempted the federal fracking rules for public lands that the Interior Department announced it intended to write in 2011 — a plan the bill's own findings acknowledge.
Would have barred the EPA from any regulation, guidance, or permit requirement covering the underground injection of fracking fluids, leaving water protection entirely to state enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the cost: people living near fracking operations on federal land — land owned by all Americans — would depend entirely on their own state's rules for water protection, with no federal floor beneath states that regulate loosely. Federal agencies (the Bureau of Land Management and EPA) would lose their authority over fracking outright.
analysis.who_pays_short: People near fracking on federal land

drawbacks.text: Removes any federal baseline: the bill's own text defines federal land to include national forests and other public lands, and on that land fracking would be regulated only by whichever state the well sits in, however strict or weak that state's rules are.

Would have preempted the first uniform federal fracking standards for public lands precisely as Interior was writing them, so drillers on land owned by all Americans would answer only to the host state.
Would have stripped the EPA of any authority over the injection of fracking fluids, so groundwater protection for federal-land drilling would rest solely on each state's enforcement capacity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: An honest supporter would argue that dual state-federal regulation is duplicative, that states have regulated oil and gas for decades and are closer to the wells, and that the bill's findings cite state and EPA studies finding no confirmed groundwater contamination from fracking itself. An honest opponent would answer that the bill arrived exactly when the Interior Department was writing the first federal fracking rules for public land, that the cited studies predate the shale boom's expansion and address only the fracturing step rather than wastewater disposal, and that a state-by-state floor means drilling next door in a neighboring state can follow weaker rules on land every taxpayer owns. On balance, the bill's benefit flows to drillers as avoided compliance costs, while its cost — removal of a federal layer of water protection on public land — would fall on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a markup, committee vote, or floor vote until the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Inhofe introduced the bill on March 28, 2012, with introductory remarks and a slate of Republican cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee that same day.

The bill was written to take effect against a specific backdrop: the Interior Department had announced in 2011 that it would promulgate new federal regulations governing hydraulic fracturing on federal land, which the bill's findings list among the reasons for the legislation.
The referral was the last action the bill ever received; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
All ten Senate sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people kept the existing federal role in overseeing fracking: the Interior Department's planned rules for public land were not preempted, and drillers gained nothing because the bill never moved. The bill's failure also left EPA's residual authority over fracking-fluid injection intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on federal fracking safeguards

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it the day it was referred to committee.

for.name: 9 of 47 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the introduction slate included Murkowski, Vitter, Sessions, Cornyn, Risch, Hoeven, and Lee.

against.name: Sen. Jeff Bingaman
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or committee vote; the record shows no committee action after referral.

against.name: Department of the Interior
against.what_they_did: Had announced in 2011 that it would write the first federal fracking rules for public lands — the rulemaking this bill was designed to preempt.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 Senate sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-led Energy Committee took no action on the bill; no Democrat ever signed on.

industries.industry: Oil and gas drillers using fracking
industries.note: The bill would have made state rules the only rules for fracking, including on federal land, sparing drillers a second federal set of standards just as Interior was preparing the first federal fracking rules for public land. The gain comes from avoiding oversight, which is the public's cost in water protection.

State regulators would have become the only regulator of fracking, including for wells on federal land owned by all Americans. Local accountability cuts toward the public; the absence of any federal floor means loosely regulated states set the terms for land every taxpayer owns.
The bill's definition covers fracking for geothermal production too, so geothermal developers on federal land would also escape federal fracking rules and follow state law only.
